reviewerByRule: Graeham C. Gillin (two-state post that states South Carolina law; never Eric Roden). The post carries no attorney attribution quote; do not add one on this refresh.
researchNotes: Federal tax law was read on law.cornell.edu/uscode (26 U.S.C. §§ 61, 67, 104, 111, 130, 5891, all HTTP 200 on 2026-09-24), IRS Publication 4345 (Rev. 9-2023, irs.gov PDF), IRS Publication 525 (irs.gov PDF), the IRS page 'Tax implications of settlements and judgments' (irs.gov/government-entities), and Commissioner v. Banks on Cornell's Supreme Court collection. Georgia statutes were read on law.justia.com (2025 Code of Georgia) through the firecrawl CLI, as in the sibling packs, because Justia returns 403 to curl and WebFetch; each year-less URL below resolved and showed the 2025 Code of Georgia breadcrumb (§ 7-4-12 and § 7-4-2 live under title-7/chapter-4/article-1; § 51-12-14 under title-51/chapter-12/article-1; §§ 48-7-20 and 48-7-27 under title-48/chapter-7/article-2). § 51-4-1, § 51-12-5.1, § 51-12-33 and § 9-3-33 are reused from facts-1651 and facts-1756 (verified 2026-09-24); the firecrawl rate limit blocked a re-read of § 51-4-1 and the URL is the one facts-1651 confirmed. South Carolina statutes were read directly on www.scstatehouse.gov (HTTP 200). Georgia's income tax rate was read from O.C.G.A. § 48-7-20(a.1) as amended effective 2026-05-11, the Governor's 2026-05-11 HB 463 release and dor.georgia.gov 'Important Tax Updates'; South Carolina's from dor.sc.gov (Individual Income page and the H. 4216 notice). S.C. Code § 15-32-530 and the 2026 indexed floor ($739,245) are reused from facts-1756 / facts-1663. All thirteen internal links, the tel: href (+18447378587, matches the profile's toll-free number) and the existing Cornell § 104 outbound link resolve (checked with a browser user agent, 0.4 s gaps). The post's four dollar figures are $250,000 (GA punitive cap, keep), $500,000 (SC punitive floor, twice, update with indexing) and $100,000 (a CPA threshold with no source, drop). No statistics are stated; data/statistics.json does not apply. Individualized-advice flags: the $100,000 CPA sentence, 'Maximizing the allocation to non-taxable categories', 'one of the most effective ways to minimize your tax liability', and the closing paragraph's 'ensuring accurate reporting'. S.C. Code § 12-6-40 adopts the Internal Revenue Code as amended through December 31, 2024; § 104 has not been amended since, so the conformity claims hold.

verifiedClaims.claim: The Internal Revenue Code § 104(a)(2) provides the foundational federal rule, but state-level tax treatment and strategic settlement structuring also play important roles.
verifiedClaims.note: The outbound Cornell link resolves (HTTP 200). Optional: soften 'strategic settlement structuring' to 'how the settlement is written', since most of a physical-injury settlement is excluded whatever its structure.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under federal law, compensation received "on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness" is excluded from gross income under IRC § 104(a)(2).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2): 'the amount of any damages (other than punitive damages) received (whether by suit or agreement and whether as lump sums or as periodic payments) on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness'
verifiedClaims.note: Verbatim match on the quoted phrase.

verifiedClaims.claim: This exclusion applies regardless of whether you receive a lump sum settlement, a structured settlement paid over time, or a jury verdict. It also applies whether the case settles before trial, during trial, or after an appeal.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2) ('whether by suit or agreement and whether as lump sums or as periodic payments'); IRS Pub. 525, Court awards and damages ('whether received in a lump sum or installments')

verifiedClaims.claim: However, if you previously deducted medical expenses on your tax returns and then receive reimbursement through a settlement, those previously deducted amounts may be taxable under the "tax benefit rule."
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 26 U.S.C. § 104(a) (opening clause: 'Except in the case of amounts attributable to (and not in excess of) deductions allowed under section 213 ... for any prior taxable year'); IRS Pub. 4345: 'you must include in income that portion of the settlement that is for medical expenses you deducted in any prior year(s) to the extent the deduction(s) provided a tax benefit'; 26 U.S.C. § 111
verifiedClaims.note: Pub. 4345 adds that the tax-benefit amount is reported as 'Other Income' on Schedule 1, line 8z, and that proceeds covering expenses paid in more than one year are allocated pro rata. Rev. Rul. 75-230 is not hosted on irs.gov; Pub. 4345 and § 104(a) carry the rule.

verifiedClaims.claim: Non-economic damages for physical pain and emotional suffering caused by a physical injury are tax-free. Georgia and South Carolina both allow recovery for pain and suffering, and these awards — which often represent the largest portion of a settlement — remain fully excluded from income under IRC § 104(a)(2).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2); IRS Pub. 4345 ('proceeds you receive for emotional distress or mental anguish attributable to a personal physical injury or physical sickness are treated the same as proceeds received for personal physical injuries'); pain-and-suffering recovery in both states reused from facts-1651 (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-6; S.C. Code § 15-32-210(9))
verifiedClaims.note: 'Often represent the largest portion' is commentary, not a sourced figure; acceptable as written.

verifiedClaims.claim: Reimbursement for vehicle repairs, replacement costs, and damage to personal property is not taxable. These payments restore you to your pre-accident position rather than providing income. If the reimbursement exceeds your adjusted basis in the property (what you originally paid), the excess could technically be a taxable gain, but this is rare in personal injury cases.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS Pub. 4345, Loss-in-value of property: 'Property settlements for loss in value of property that are less than the adjusted basis of your property are not taxable ... If the property settlement exceeds your adjusted basis in the property, the excess is income.'
verifiedClaims.note: Pub. 4345 also says you must reduce your basis in the property by the settlement. 'What you originally paid' is a loose gloss on adjusted basis (cost adjusted for improvements and depreciation); acceptable for a general-information post.

verifiedClaims.claim: Compensation paid to a spouse for loss of companionship, affection, and support resulting from the injured person's physical injuries is generally not taxable when it originates from a physical injury claim.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2) (damages 'on account of' personal physical injuries); H.R. Conf. Rep. No. 104-737 (1996), Small Business Job Protection Act § 1605 (damages for loss of consortium due to the physical injury of a spouse are excludable); IRS 'Tax implications of settlements and judgments' page
verifiedClaims.note: The exclusion of consortium damages rests on the 1996 conference report, not on text restated in Pub. 4345; the post's 'generally' hedge is right.

verifiedClaims.claim: Settlements and verdicts in wrongful death cases are generally tax-free under IRC § 104(a)(2) because they arise from a physical injury (the death).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2); IRS 'Tax implications of settlements and judgments' (compensatory wrongful-death damages excluded; punitive damages excluded only where state law provides only for punitive damages, § 104(c))
verifiedClaims.note: Compensatory wrongful-death damages are excluded; any punitive/exemplary component is not (see the next row).

verifiedClaims.claim: Both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-1) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-51-10) wrongful death statutes allow surviving family members to recover damages that are excluded from federal income tax.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The exclusion comes from federal law, not from either state statute. Georgia measures the claim by 'the full value of the life of the decedent' (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-1(1); the cause of action is § 51-4-2). South Carolina's § 15-51-10 creates the action, and § 15-51-40 lets the jury add 'exemplary damages when the wrongful act, neglect, or default was the result of recklessness, wilfulness, or malice' — that exemplary component is punitive and taxable. The § 104(c) exception (punitive damages excluded where state law allows only punitive damages in a wrongful-death action) does not apply in Georgia or South Carolina, because both allow compensatory recovery.
verifiedClaims.note: Both citations resolve and are the right sections. Reword: 'Compensatory damages recovered under Georgia's wrongful death statute (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-1) and South Carolina's (S.C. Code § 15-51-10) are excluded from federal income tax; a South Carolina jury's exemplary damages under S.C. Code § 15-51-40 are punitive and remain taxable.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Compensation for wages you would have earned had the accident not occurred is generally taxable as ordinary income. The IRS reasons that these wages would have been taxed if you had earned them normally. This applies to both past lost wages and future lost earning capacity.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Wrong for a physical-injury case. Lost wages and lost earning capacity recovered on account of a personal physical injury are excluded under § 104(a)(2). IRS: 'The Service has consistently held that compensatory damages, including lost wages, received on account of a personal physical injury are excludable from gross income with the exception of punitive damages.' Pub. 4345 lists lost wages as taxable only 'if you receive a settlement in an employment-related lawsuit; for example, for unlawful discrimination or involuntary termination'. Pub. 525's 'lost wages or lost profits in most cases' item is the general rule that § 104(a)(2) overrides for physical-injury recoveries ('Don't include in your income compensatory damages for personal physical injury or physical sickness').
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS, 'Tax implications of settlements and judgments'; IRS Pub. 4345, Lost wages or lost profits; IRS Pub. 525, Court awards and damages; 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2)
verifiedClaims.note: The most consequential error on the page. It repeats in the comparison table, the Georgia and South Carolina rate bullets, the allocation paragraph, the medical-malpractice bullet, the excerpt, the key takeaways, faq:0, faq:1 and faq:4. Rewrite the section: 'Lost wages and lost earning capacity that are part of a physical-injury settlement are excluded along with the rest of the recovery (IRC § 104(a)(2)); the IRS treats them as compensation for the injury, not as wages. Lost wages become taxable only when the underlying claim is not a physical injury — an employment claim such as wrongful termination or discrimination, or lost profits of a business.'

verifiedClaims.claim: The settlement agreement should clearly separate lost wage damages from other categories to ensure proper tax treatment.
verifiedClaims.note: Rests on the lost-wages error; no separation is needed because the wage component of a physical-injury settlement is excluded with the rest. Delete, or replace with the general allocation point already made under 'Allocate Damages Carefully'.

verifiedClaims.claim: If you receive compensation for emotional distress that does not originate from a physical injury, the award is taxable. However, if your emotional distress stems directly from a physical injury — for example, anxiety and depression following a traumatic brain injury — the compensation remains tax-free.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 26 U.S.C. § 104(a) flush language: 'For purposes of paragraph (2), emotional distress shall not be treated as a physical injury or physical sickness. The preceding sentence shall not apply to an amount of damages not in excess of the amount paid for medical care ... attributable to emotional distress.' IRS Pub. 4345, Emotional distress or mental anguish
verifiedClaims.note: Optional precision: the taxable amount is reduced by medical costs paid for the emotional distress (§ 104(a) flush language; Pub. 4345).

verifiedClaims.claim: The distinction matters: emotional distress from witnessing an accident (without personal physical injury) is taxable, while emotional distress caused by your own injuries is not.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 26 U.S.C. § 104(a) flush language; IRS Pub. 525, Emotional distress ('Emotional distress itself isn't a physical injury or physical sickness, but damages you receive for emotional distress due to a physical injury or sickness are treated as received for the physical injury or sickness')

verifiedClaims.claim: Punitive damages are always taxable, regardless of the underlying claim. These damages are intended to punish the defendant rather than compensate the plaintiff, and the IRS treats them as income.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Taxable, with one narrow statutory exception: § 104(c) keeps the exclusion for punitive damages in a wrongful-death action where the applicable state law (as of September 13, 1995) allows only punitive damages in such an action. Neither Georgia nor South Carolina is such a state, so in this firm's cases punitive damages are taxable. Pub. 4345: 'Punitive damages are taxable ... even if the punitive damages were received in a settlement for personal physical injuries or physical sickness.'
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2), (c); IRS Pub. 4345, Punitive Damages; IRS 'Tax implications of settlements and judgments' ('Punitive damages are not excludable from gross income, with one exception')
verifiedClaims.note: Change 'always taxable, regardless of the underlying claim' to 'taxable even when they arise from a physical-injury claim; the one exception in the Code (IRC § 104(c), for states whose wrongful death law allows only punitive damages) does not apply in Georgia or South Carolina'. Same fix in faq:2.

verifiedClaims.claim: In Georgia, punitive damages are capped at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1)
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(g) ($250,000 cap); (e) no cap in product liability; (f) no cap, against the active tort-feasor only, for specific intent to harm or substantial impairment by alcohol or drugs — reused from facts-1756 (verified 2026-09-24)
verifiedClaims.note: 'In most cases' is the right hedge. Optional: '(no cap in product liability cases or where the defendant intended harm or was substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: while South Carolina allows punitive damages up to three times compensatory damages or $500,000, whichever is greater (S.C. Code § 15-32-530)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000 under § 15-32-530(A), but (D) indexes the dollar floor to CPI every year — $739,245 for 2026 (S.C. RFA memo 2026-02-03). A higher tier (four times or $2,000,000) applies under (B), and there is no cap under (C) where the defendant intended harm, has pled guilty to or been convicted of a felony arising from the same conduct, or was substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-32-530(A)-(D) (read on scstatehouse.gov 2026-09-24); 2026 indexed figure reused from facts-1756 / facts-1663 (S.C. RFA memo, 2026-02-03)
verifiedClaims.note: Change to 'the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000 — a floor indexed for inflation each year, $739,245 in 2026 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530)'. Same fix in the South Carolina bullet, the key takeaways, faq:1 and faq:2.

verifiedClaims.claim: Even though they arise from a personal injury case, punitive damages must be reported as "Other Income" on your federal tax return.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS Pub. 4345: 'Punitive damages are taxable and should be reported as "Other Income" on line 8z of Form 1040, Schedule 1'
verifiedClaims.note: Optional pinpoint: 'on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8z'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Pre-judgment and post-judgment interest added to your award is taxable as ordinary income.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS Pub. 4345: 'Interest on any settlement is generally taxable as "Interest Income"'; IRS Pub. 525, Court awards and damages, item 1: 'Interest on any award'

verifiedClaims.claim: Even if the underlying damages are tax-free, any interest component is treated as investment income by the IRS.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Treated as interest income, reported on Form 1040, line 2b (Pub. 4345). 'Investment income' is not the IRS's term.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS Pub. 4345, Interest
verifiedClaims.note: Change 'investment income' to 'interest income'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia allows pre-judgment interest at 7% per year (O.C.G.A. § 7-4-12), and South Carolina allows it at the statutory rate.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Wrong statute and wrong rate. O.C.G.A. § 7-4-12 is post-judgment interest: 'All judgments in this state shall bear annual interest upon the principal amount recovered at a rate equal to the prime rate as published by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System ... on the day the judgment is entered plus 3 percent' (§ 7-4-12(a)). Pre-judgment interest on unliquidated tort damages in Georgia is available only under the Unliquidated Damages Interest Act, O.C.G.A. § 51-12-14: after a written demand the defendant does not pay within 30 days, and only if the judgment is not less than the amount demanded, at 'the prime rate ... plus 3 percent' from the thirtieth day after the demand until judgment (§ 51-12-14(a), (c)). The 7% figure is the general legal rate 'where the rate percent is not established by written contract' (O.C.G.A. § 7-4-2(a)(1)(A)), which does not govern tort judgments. South Carolina: a judgment draws interest at 'the prime rate as listed in the first edition of the Wall Street Journal published for each calendar year ... plus four percentage points, compounded annually' (S.C. Code § 34-31-20(B)); the 8.75% legal rate in § 34-31-20(A) applies to accounts stated and liquidated sums, not to unliquidated injury damages, so South Carolina personal-injury awards generally carry post-judgment interest only.
verifiedClaims.note: Second most consequential error: a wrong rate tied to the wrong statute. Rewrite: 'In Georgia, a judgment earns post-judgment interest at the federal prime rate plus 3% (O.C.G.A. § 7-4-12), and pre-judgment interest is available only after a formal written demand under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-14; in South Carolina a judgment earns the Wall Street Journal prime rate plus four percentage points, compounded annually (S.C. Code § 34-31-20(B)). Whatever the rate, the interest is taxable.' § 51-12-14: https://law.justia.com/codes/georgia/title-51/chapter-12/article-1/section-51-12-14/ ; § 34-31-20: https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t34c031.php

verifiedClaims.claim: If you itemized medical expenses on a prior year's tax return and later receive a settlement reimbursing those same expenses, the reimbursed amount may be taxable under the tax benefit rule. You only need to include the amount that provided a tax benefit in the prior year.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS Pub. 4345 ('to the extent the deduction(s) provided a tax benefit'); 26 U.S.C. § 104(a) opening clause; 26 U.S.C. § 111
verifiedClaims.note: Duplicates the medical-expenses subsection; harmless.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia follows the federal IRC § 104(a)(2) exclusion, so damages excluded at the federal level are also excluded from Georgia state income tax.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 48-7-27(a): 'Georgia taxable net income of an individual shall be the taxpayer's federal adjusted gross income, as defined in the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, less' the listed adjustments — none adds back § 104 damages
verifiedClaims.note: Optional citation: '(Georgia starts from federal adjusted gross income, O.C.G.A. § 48-7-27)'. The Justia page is headed '[Effective July 1, 2026; Effective until January 1, 2027]' — subsection (a) is unchanged.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia's income tax rate is a flat 5.49% (as of 2025), which applies to taxable components like lost wages and punitive damages.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 4.99% for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026 (O.C.G.A. § 48-7-20(a.1), as rewritten by HB 463, signed May 11, 2026, with further 0.125-point annual reductions from 2027 toward 3.99%, subject to delay triggers). The rate was 5.19% for 2025 (HB 111) and 5.39% for 2024; 5.49% was the rate for 2024 under the original HB 1437 schedule before the 2024 amendment. Taxable components in a physical-injury case are punitive damages and interest, not lost wages.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 48-7-20(a.1) and amendment notes (2025 Code of Georgia via Justia); Office of the Governor, 'Gov. Kemp Signs Legislation Lowering Taxes' (2026-05-11: 'HB 463 lowers Georgia's state income tax rate from 5.19% to 4.99%, beginning January 1, 2026'); dor.georgia.gov, Important Tax Updates ('The Georgia income tax rate has been reduced to a flat rate of 4.99%')
verifiedClaims.note: Change to: 'Georgia's income tax is a flat 4.99% for 2026 (O.C.G.A. § 48-7-20), which applies to the taxable pieces of a recovery such as punitive damages and interest.' Mirror in the comparison table.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule — you can recover if you are less than 50% at fault, but your award is reduced by your percentage of fault. The reduced amount remains subject to the same tax rules.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(a), (g) ('the plaintiff shall not be entitled to receive any damages if the plaintiff is 50 percent or more responsible') — reused from facts-1756 / facts-2647
verifiedClaims.note: Matches the writer-profile jurisdiction table.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia allows 2 years to file a personal injury claim (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33 (two-year limitation for injuries to the person) — reused from facts-1756 / facts-1649
verifiedClaims.note: The tail 'Filing promptly ensures you preserve the right to recover tax-free compensation' is commentary.

verifiedClaims.claim: Workers' compensation benefits in Georgia are entirely tax-free under both federal and state law, including temporary total disability and permanent partial disability payments.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(1) ('amounts received under workmen's compensation acts as compensation for personal injuries or sickness'); IRS Pub. 525, Workers' Compensation; Georgia conformity via O.C.G.A. § 48-7-27(a)
verifiedClaims.note: Pub. 525 caveat (already covered later in the post): the part of workers' compensation that offsets Social Security benefits is treated as Social Security benefits and may be taxable.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina generally follows federal tax treatment for personal injury settlements, meaning amounts excluded under IRC § 104(a)(2) are also excluded from SC state income tax.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 12-6-40(A)(1)(a) (adopts the Internal Revenue Code 'as amended through December 31, 2024'); § 12-6-1110 (gross income, AGI and taxable income 'as calculated under the Internal Revenue Code are modified as provided in this article'); SCDOR: for 2026 'Federal Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) is now the starting point for the South Carolina Individual Income Tax return' (previously federal taxable income)
verifiedClaims.note: § 104 has not been amended since the 2024 conformity date, so the exclusion carries through.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina's top marginal rate is 6.4% for taxable portions of your settlement, slightly higher than Georgia's rate.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: For tax year 2026, South Carolina taxes income under $30,000 at 1.99% and income of $30,000 and above at 5.21% (H. 4216, signed March 30, 2026, replacing the prior three-bracket structure), with further reductions when revenue growth reaches 5%. The top rate was 6% for 2025 and 6.2% for 2024; 6.4% was the 2023 rate. 5.21% is still slightly higher than Georgia's 4.99%.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDOR, 'Information about H. 4216' ('The tax rate for income less than $30,000 is 1.99%. The tax rate for income from $30,000 and above is 5.21%, minus $966.'); SCDOR Individual Income Tax page ('The 2025 top marginal Individual Income Tax rate is 6% on taxable income'); S.C. Code § 12-6-510(B)
verifiedClaims.note: Change to: 'For 2026, South Carolina taxes income above $30,000 at 5.21% (1.99% below that), slightly higher than Georgia's 4.99%.' Mirror in the comparison table.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina uses a modified comparative fault system where you can recover damages if you are less than 51% at fault, providing slightly more latitude than Georgia's 50% threshold.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (S.C. 1991) — plaintiff recovers if his or her negligence is 'not greater than' the defendant's; reused from facts-1756
verifiedClaims.note: Correct and correctly uncited to any statute. If a citation is added it must be Nelson, never § 15-38-15 (profile rule).

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina allows 3 years to file personal injury claims (S.C. Code § 15-3-530), giving more time to structure a tax-efficient settlement.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-3-530(5) (three years, injury to the person) — reused from facts-1756 / facts-1649
verifiedClaims.note: The deadline is right. The clause 'giving more time to structure a tax-efficient settlement' is filler with no tax content; optional trim to 'S.C. Code § 15-3-530'.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina workers' compensation benefits are also fully tax-exempt at both the federal and state level.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(1); S.C. Code § 12-6-40 conformity

verifiedClaims.claim: SC caps punitive damages at three times compensatory damages or $500,000, whichever is greater (S.C. Code § 15-32-530). These remain fully taxable regardless of the cap.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000, indexed each year ($739,245 in 2026) under § 15-32-530(A), (D); higher tier and uncapped cases under (B), (C). Taxability is unaffected by the cap.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-32-530; 2026 indexed floor reused from facts-1756 (S.C. RFA memo 2026-02-03)
verifiedClaims.note: Add '(indexed each year; $739,245 in 2026)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Strategic settlement structuring is one of the most effective ways to minimize your tax liability.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Overstated for a physical-injury case, where the compensatory recovery is excluded whatever its structure; structure matters only for the taxable pieces (punitive damages, interest, non-physical claims) and for how periodic payments are set up. Reads as individualized tax advice.
verifiedClaims.note: Advice-tone flag. Suggested: 'How the settlement is written matters for the parts of a recovery that can be taxed.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Maximizing the allocation to non-taxable categories (medical expenses, pain and suffering, physical impairment) while accurately reflecting taxable categories (lost wages, punitive damages) can significantly reduce your tax bill. The IRS respects reasonable allocations agreed upon by the parties, but may challenge allocations that appear designed solely to avoid taxes.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Pub. 4345: 'A settlement payment may consist of multiple elements that have been allocated by the parties ... Generally, the IRS will not disturb an allocation if it is consistent with the substance of the settled claims.' The IRS page adds: 'The IRS is reluctant to override the intent of the parties.' The second sentence is therefore sound; the first is wrong on lost wages (excluded in a physical-injury case) and 'maximizing' reads as advice to shift allocations rather than reflect the claims.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS Pub. 4345 (introduction); IRS 'Tax implications of settlements and judgments'; 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2)
verifiedClaims.note: Advice-tone flag. Rewrite: 'An agreement that states what each part of the payment is for — medical expenses, pain and suffering, lost income from the injury, and separately any punitive damages or interest — gives the IRS a record to follow. The IRS generally will not disturb an allocation that is consistent with the substance of the settled claims, but an allocation that does not match the claims can be challenged.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Structured settlements offer several tax advantages: the investment income earned within the annuity is tax-free (unlike a lump sum invested independently), payments can be tailored to your financial needs, and the arrangement provides long-term financial security.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2) (damages excluded 'whether as lump sums or as periodic payments'); 26 U.S.C. § 130 (qualified assignment of a liability to make periodic payments as damages on account of personal injury 'in a case involving physical injury or physical sickness'); 26 U.S.C. § 5891 (40% excise tax on factoring a structured settlement without a court-approved qualified order)
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate as a general statement: when the periodic payments are themselves the damages (the claimant does not own the annuity, § 130 qualified assignment), the full payments including the growth are excluded, whereas income earned on a lump sum the claimant invests is taxable. Optional caution worth one sentence: selling future structured-settlement payments requires court approval, and a purchaser who buys them without it owes a 40% excise tax (IRC § 5891).

verifiedClaims.claim: If your case involves both physical injury claims and related non-physical claims (such as a defamation claim arising from the same incident), negotiating separate settlement amounts for each ensures the physical injury compensation remains tax-free while only the non-physical portion is taxed.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS Pub. 4345 (allocation by the parties; emotional distress not from physical injury taxable); IRS Pub. 525 ('injury to reputation' example); 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2)
verifiedClaims.note: Soften 'ensures' to 'helps make clear'; the allocation must still be consistent with the substance of the claims.

verifiedClaims.claim: Lost wages Taxable Taxable (5.49%) Taxable (up to 6.4%)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Lost wages that are part of a physical-injury settlement: Not taxable / Not taxable / Not taxable. If a rate row is wanted, attach it to the punitive-damages and interest rows instead: Georgia 4.99% (2026); South Carolina 5.21% on income of $30,000 and above (2026).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS 'Tax implications of settlements and judgments'; O.C.G.A. § 48-7-20(a.1); SCDOR H. 4216 notice
verifiedClaims.note: Rename the row 'Lost wages (from the physical injury)' so the exclusion reads correctly; a separate row 'Lost wages (employment claim, no physical injury)' can stay Taxable if the writer wants the contrast.

verifiedClaims.claim: Comparison-table rows for medical expenses, pain and suffering, property damage, emotional distress (from physical injury) — Not taxable; emotional distress (no physical injury), punitive damages, interest on award — Taxable; workers' comp benefits — Not taxable, in all three columns.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(1), (a)(2) and flush language; IRS Pub. 4345; state conformity via O.C.G.A. § 48-7-27(a) and S.C. Code § 12-6-40
verifiedClaims.note: State columns follow federal because both states start from federal AGI (Georgia § 48-7-27(a); South Carolina from tax year 2026, per SCDOR) or federal taxable income (South Carolina through 2025).

verifiedClaims.claim: Wrongful death cases — generally tax-free, but any punitive damage component and pre-judgment interest remain taxable.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Tax rule is right (punitive damages and interest taxable). 'Pre-judgment interest' is the wrong label for this firm's states: South Carolina personal-injury and wrongful-death judgments generally carry post-judgment interest only (S.C. Code § 34-31-20(B)), and Georgia pre-judgment interest exists only under the § 51-12-14 demand procedure. Say 'interest'.
verifiedClaims.note: Change 'pre-judgment interest' to 'interest on a judgment'. Also see the wrongful-death subsection: South Carolina exemplary damages under § 15-51-40 are the punitive component.

verifiedClaims.claim: Medical malpractice claims — may involve large future medical expense awards that are tax-free, but lost earning capacity is taxable.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Lost earning capacity recovered on account of the physical injury is excluded under § 104(a)(2), like lost wages.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS 'Tax implications of settlements and judgments' ('compensatory damages, including lost wages, received on account of a personal physical injury are excludable'); 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2)
verifiedClaims.note: Rewrite the tail: 'and future lost earning capacity is excluded along with them; the taxable pieces, if any, are punitive damages and interest.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Workers' compensation cases — benefits are entirely tax-free, but if you receive both workers' comp and Social Security Disability, the combined amount may trigger taxation of a portion of your SSDI benefits.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS Pub. 525, Workers' Compensation: 'If part of your workers' compensation reduces your social security or equivalent railroad retirement benefits received, that part is considered social security (or equivalent railroad retirement) benefits and may be taxable.'
verifiedClaims.note: The mechanism is the Social Security offset: the offset portion of workers' compensation is treated as Social Security benefits. The post's wording is an acceptable plain-English version.

verifiedClaims.claim: commercial property claims may include taxable business interruption damages
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS Pub. 4345, Lost wages or lost profits ('If you receive a settlement for lost profits from your trade or business, the portion of the proceeds attributable to the carrying on of your trade or business is net earnings subject to self-employment tax'); IRS Pub. 525, item 5(c) 'Interference with business operations'

verifiedClaims.claim: Consider consulting a tax professional: For settlements exceeding $100,000, working with a CPA or tax attorney alongside your personal injury lawyer ensures optimal tax treatment.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No source sets a $100,000 threshold; the figure is invented and 'ensures optimal tax treatment' is individualized advice. Pub. 4345's only threshold is the $1,000 estimated-tax trigger, which is unrelated.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS Pub. 4345 (no such threshold)
verifiedClaims.note: Advice-tone flag and the one unsourced dollar figure. Replace with: 'Consider consulting a tax professional: if any part of your recovery is taxable — punitive damages, interest, or previously deducted medical expenses — a CPA or tax attorney can tell you how to report it and whether estimated payments are needed.'

verifiedClaims.claim: File on time: In Georgia, you have 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and in South Carolina, 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) to file your claim.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33; S.C. Code § 15-3-530(5) — reused from facts-1756 / facts-1649
verifiedClaims.note: Matches the writer-profile jurisdiction table.

verifiedClaims.claim: At Roden Law, our attorneys understand the tax implications of settlement structuring and work to maximize the non-taxable portions of your award while ensuring accurate reporting of any taxable components.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Firm statement, not verifiable against a source. 'Ensuring accurate reporting' implies the firm prepares or vouches for the client's tax return; 'maximize the non-taxable portions' echoes the allocation-shifting advice flagged above.
verifiedClaims.note: Advice-tone flag. Suggested: 'At Roden Law, our attorneys understand which parts of a recovery can be taxed, write settlement agreements that state what each payment is for, and will point you to a tax professional for anything that must be reported.'

verifiedClaims.claim: We handle personal injury cases across Georgia and South Carolina on a contingency fee basis — you pay nothing unless we recover compensation for you. If you have been injured in an accident and want to understand the full value of your claim, including tax implications, contact Roden Law for a free consultation or call 1-844-RESULTS.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: profiles/writer-profile.md (toll-free line 1-844-RESULTS is tel:+18447378587; contingency-fee trust signal)

Banks, 543 U.S. 426 (2005), when a recovery is taxable the plaintiff's income includes the share paid to the attorney as a contingent fee, and the miscellaneous itemized deduction that once offset it remains disallowed — Pub. L. 119-21 § 70110 (2025) struck the 'before January 1, 2026' sunset from what is now 26 U.S.C. § 67(h).

verifiedClaims.claim: Most personal injury settlements are tax-free under IRC § 104(a)(2), including compensation for medical expenses, pain and suffering, and property damage. Lost wages, punitive damages (capped at $250,000 in Georgia under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1 and three times compensatory in South Carolina under S.C. Code § 15-32-530), and interest are taxable. Strategic settlement structuring and proper damage allocation can significantly reduce your tax burden.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Lost wages recovered for a physical injury are excluded, not taxable. South Carolina's cap is the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000, indexed each year ($739,245 in 2026); 'three times compensatory' alone misstates it. The closing sentence overstates what structuring does for a mostly excluded recovery.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS 'Tax implications of settlements and judgments'; 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2); O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(g); S.C. Code § 15-32-530(A), (D)
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'Most personal injury settlements are tax-free under IRC § 104(a)(2), including compensation for medical expenses, pain and suffering, lost wages from the injury, and property damage. Punitive damages (capped at $250,000 in most Georgia cases under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1, and at the greater of three times compensatory damages or an inflation-indexed $500,000 — $739,245 in 2026 — under S.C. Code § 15-32-530), interest on a judgment, and emotional-distress damages with no physical injury are taxable. A settlement agreement that states what each payment is for makes the tax treatment clear.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Which parts of a personal injury settlement are taxable and which are not, and where the line falls for lost wages and punitive damages.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The excerpt itself states no false fact, but it frames lost wages as a borderline item; after the correction the line falls at punitive damages, interest and non-physical claims. This text publishes as the Article schema description.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS 'Tax implications of settlements and judgments'; IRS Pub. 4345
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'Which parts of a personal injury settlement are taxable and which are not, why lost wages from an injury usually are not, and where the line falls for punitive damages and interest.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Most personal injury settlement proceeds are not taxable in Georgia. Compensation for medical expenses, pain and suffering, and property damage is excluded from federal and Georgia state income tax under IRC § 104(a)(2). However, lost wages, punitive damages, and interest on the award are typically taxable.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Lost wages that are part of a physical-injury settlement are excluded; punitive damages and interest are taxable. Georgia conformity rests on O.C.G.A. § 48-7-27(a) (federal AGI starting point), not on § 104(a)(2) itself.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS 'Tax implications of settlements and judgments'; 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2); O.C.G.A. § 48-7-27(a)
verifiedClaims.note: Renders into FAQPage structured data. Suggested: '... Compensation for medical expenses, pain and suffering, lost wages from the injury, and property damage is excluded from federal income tax under IRC § 104(a)(2), and Georgia follows the federal figure (O.C.G.A. § 48-7-27). Punitive damages and interest on the award are taxable.'

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina follows federal tax treatment, so compensation for physical injuries is generally tax-free. Taxable components include lost wages, punitive damages (capped at three times compensatory damages or $500,000 under S.C. Code § 15-32-530), and pre-judgment interest.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Lost wages from the injury are excluded. The cap is the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000, indexed each year ($739,245 in 2026). South Carolina injury judgments generally carry post-judgment interest (S.C. Code § 34-31-20(B), prime plus four percentage points), not pre-judgment interest; say 'interest on a judgment'. Conformity: S.C. Code § 12-6-40.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS 'Tax implications of settlements and judgments'; S.C. Code §§ 12-6-40, 15-32-530(A), (D), 34-31-20(B); 2026 indexed floor reused from facts-1756
verifiedClaims.note: Renders into FAQPage structured data. Suggested: 'South Carolina follows federal tax treatment (S.C. Code § 12-6-40), so compensation for physical injuries — including lost wages from the injury — is generally tax-free. Taxable components are punitive damages (capped at the greater of three times compensatory damages or an inflation-indexed $500,000, $739,245 in 2026, under S.C. Code § 15-32-530) and interest on a judgment.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. Punitive damages are always taxable as ordinary income regardless of the underlying claim type. They must be reported as Other Income on your federal tax return. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1), and South Carolina caps them at three times compensatory or $500,000.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Taxable in a Georgia or South Carolina car-accident case; the only statutory exception (§ 104(c), wrongful-death actions in states whose law allows only punitive damages) does not apply in either state. Reported as Other Income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8z. South Carolina: greater of three times compensatory or $500,000, indexed ($739,245 in 2026).
verifiedClaims.note: Renders into FAQPage structured data. Suggested: 'Yes. Punitive damages are taxable as ordinary income even when they come from a physical-injury claim, and are reported as Other Income on your federal return. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1); South Carolina caps them at the greater of three times compensatory damages or an inflation-indexed $500,000 — $739,245 in 2026 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).'

verifiedClaims.claim: No. Pain and suffering compensation arising from a physical injury is excluded from federal income tax under IRC § 104(a)(2). This applies in both Georgia and South Carolina and covers both economic and non-economic damages directly tied to your physical injuries.
verifiedClaims.note: Correct. The last clause is slightly muddled (pain and suffering is itself non-economic) but true — the exclusion covers both economic and non-economic compensatory damages on account of the injury. Optional: 'and the same exclusion covers the economic damages tied to your physical injuries'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. Lost wages received as part of a personal injury settlement are generally taxable as ordinary income because the wages would have been taxed if you had earned them normally. Your attorney can help structure the settlement agreement to properly allocate and minimize the tax impact.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Usually no. Lost wages recovered on account of a personal physical injury are excluded under IRC § 104(a)(2): 'The Service has consistently held that compensatory damages, including lost wages, received on account of a personal physical injury are excludable from gross income with the exception of punitive damages.' Lost wages are taxable when the claim is not a physical injury — an employment claim (Pub. 4345: 'a settlement in an employment-related lawsuit; for example, for unlawful discrimination or involuntary termination').
verifiedClaims.sourceName: IRS 'Tax implications of settlements and judgments'; IRS Pub. 4345, Lost wages or lost profits; 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2)
verifiedClaims.note: The question is 'Are lost wages from a settlement taxable?' and the published answer is 'Yes.' The IRS's answer for a physical-injury settlement is no. This answer also publishes as FAQPage structured data, so the wrong answer is published twice. Keep the question; change the answer to open 'Usually no.' and drop the 'minimize the tax impact' sentence.

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. A structured settlement pays compensation over time through an annuity, and the investment income earned within the annuity is tax-free — unlike a lump sum that you invest independently. This is particularly beneficial for large settlements involving lifetime care needs from brain injuries or spinal cord injuries.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2) ('whether as lump sums or as periodic payments'); 26 U.S.C. § 130 (qualified assignment); 26 U.S.C. § 5891
verifiedClaims.note: Renders into FAQPage structured data. Accurate as a general statement when the periodic payments are the damages under the settlement (§ 130 qualified assignment). 'Particularly beneficial' is opinion; acceptable.

recommendedEdits: Lost wages section ('Lost Wages and Lost Earning Capacity'): reverse the rule — lost wages and lost earning capacity recovered on account of a physical injury are excluded under IRC § 104(a)(2) (IRS: 'compensatory damages, including lost wages, received on account of a personal physical injury are excludable'); lost wages are taxable only in employment-type claims with no physical injury (Pub. 4345). Consider moving the subsection under 'What Parts of a Settlement Are Not Taxable?'.
Delete 'The settlement agreement should clearly separate lost wage damages from other categories to ensure proper tax treatment.'
Comparison table: change the 'Lost wages' row to Not taxable in all three columns (label it 'Lost wages (from the physical injury)'); remove the 5.49% and 6.4% figures from that row.

Georgia rate bullet: replace 'flat 5.49% (as of 2025)' with 'flat 4.99% for 2026 (O.C.G.A. § 48-7-20)' and replace 'taxable components like lost wages and punitive damages' with 'taxable components such as punitive damages and interest'.

South Carolina rate bullet: replace 'top marginal rate is 6.4%' with 'For 2026, South Carolina taxes income above $30,000 at 5.21% (1.99% below that)'; keep 'slightly higher than Georgia's rate' (5.21% vs 4.99%).

Interest section: replace 'Georgia allows pre-judgment interest at 7% per year (O.C.G.A. § 7-4-12), and South Carolina allows it at the statutory rate.' with 'In Georgia, a judgment earns post-judgment interest at the federal prime rate plus 3% (O.C.G.A. § 7-4-12), and pre-judgment interest is available only after a formal written demand under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-14; in South Carolina a judgment earns the prime rate plus four percentage points, compounded annually (S.C. Code § 34-31-20(B)). Whatever the rate, the interest is taxable.'
Interest section: change 'treated as investment income by the IRS' to 'reported as interest income'.

Punitive damages section and faq:2: replace 'always taxable, regardless of the underlying claim' with 'taxable even when they arise from a physical-injury claim; the one exception in the Code (IRC § 104(c), for states whose wrongful death law allows only punitive damages) does not apply in Georgia or South Carolina'.

South Carolina punitive cap (body twice, keyTakeaways, faq:1, faq:2): state it as 'the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000, a floor indexed for inflation each year — $739,245 in 2026 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530)'; the key takeaways must not say 'three times compensatory' alone.

Wrongful death subsection: reword the second sentence so the exclusion is attributed to federal law and note that South Carolina exemplary damages under S.C. Code § 15-51-40 are punitive and taxable; keep the § 51-4-1 and § 15-51-10 citations.

Case-types list: in the wrongful death bullet change 'pre-judgment interest' to 'interest on a judgment'; in the medical malpractice bullet replace 'but lost earning capacity is taxable' with 'and future lost earning capacity is excluded along with them'.

Allocation paragraph: drop 'lost wages' from the taxable list and replace 'Maximizing the allocation to non-taxable categories' with wording about stating what each payment is for; keep the sentence that the IRS generally will not disturb an allocation consistent with the substance of the settled claims (Pub. 4345).
Soften 'Strategic settlement structuring is one of the most effective ways to minimize your tax liability' to 'How the settlement is written matters for the parts of a recovery that can be taxed'.
Steps list, item 4: delete the $100,000 threshold and 'ensures optimal tax treatment'; recommend a tax professional when any part of the recovery is taxable.

Closing paragraph: replace 'work to maximize the non-taxable portions of your award while ensuring accurate reporting of any taxable components' with wording that the firm writes agreements stating what each payment is for and refers taxable pieces to a tax professional.
Excerpt: reframe so lost wages sit on the excluded side ('why lost wages from an injury usually are not [taxable]') and the line falls at punitive damages and interest.
keyTakeaways: move lost wages to the excluded list, fix the South Carolina cap wording, and replace the 'significantly reduce your tax burden' sentence.
faq:0, faq:1, faq:4: move lost wages to the excluded side; faq:4 must open 'Usually no.'; faq:1 'pre-judgment interest' becomes 'interest on a judgment'.

Optional one-sentence addition under the taxable-components section: when part of a recovery is taxable, the taxable amount includes the share paid to the attorney as a contingent fee (Commissioner v. Banks, 543 U.S. 426 (2005)), and the miscellaneous itemized deduction that once offset such fees remains disallowed (26 U.S.C. § 67(h), made permanent by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70110 in 2025).

Optional one-sentence caution in the structured-settlement subsection: selling future structured-settlement payments requires court approval, and a purchaser without it owes a 40% excise tax (IRC § 5891).
